speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)):
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-143
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I move:
That, in relation to Bill C-143, An Act to provide supplementary borrowing authority, one sitting day shall be allotted to the consideration of each of the report stage and the third reading of the Bill; and
That fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business on those days, any proceedings before the House shall be interrupted, if required, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question then necessary in order to dispose of the stage of the Bill then under consideration shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
He said: Madam Speaker, on March 8 when I addressed second reading of Bill C-143, An Act to provide supplementary borrowing authority, I described the Bill as a measure required by the Government for prudent financial housekeeping. 1 might add that since debate began on this Bill more than a month ago, we have spent more than 33 hours, involving nine days, to take the matter to this stage. This total includes an aggregate of close to 24 hours of debate in this House, and a further ten hours before the House Standing Committee on Finance.
Again as I pointed out at that time, the interim borrowing authority we are seeking is normally a routine procedure which gives the Government economic leverage in the marketplace. Without this authorization, the borrowing activities of the Government would be constrained in the early months of the new fiscal year, which is traditionally a period in which the Government usually faces heavy cash requirements stemming, for example, from payment of income tax refunds and from other seasonal factors.
What we have attempted to point out during this protracted debate on this matter is that if borrowing powers are limited during this crucial time, the Government would be precluded from the prudent planning of its debt program and would not be able to take advantage of developing market situations. This would be costly not only to the Government, but could impact upon provincial Governments in their borrowing activities and could impact also upon the private sector in the market, and therefore be disruptive in the capital market generally.
I would remind Hon. Members that in the tabling of the Main Estimates more than a month ago, the President of the
March 24, 1983

Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) did give ample indication of how the money under discussion would be spent. 1 would remind Hon. Members as well that almost two-thirds of those budgetary estimates are slated for statutory expenditures based on continuing authority given by Acts of the current and previous Parliaments which determine the basis whereby individuals, businesses, provincial and other Governments in Canada become entitled to receive federal funds.
The Main Estimates show in great detail the wide variety of programs being carried on by the Government of Canada in meeting its responsibilities of assisting Canadians in a very difficult time. We know that the signs are that this has been a struggle that seems to be paying off, that there is an improvement in the economy, but it is a struggle against a world-wide and very, very difficult recession.
The Estimates reflect a 21 per cent rise in cash payments under the Established Programs Financing Act whereby the federal Government contributes to such things as financing of hospital insurance, medicare, extended health care and postsecondary education. They indicate a $2.9 billion allocation to Unemployment Insurance, as we anticipate a slow recovery in employment prospects during our gradual recovery from the recession. The Estimates show a further 21 per cent increase in federal contributions under the Canada Assistance Plan. This plan provides, for example, for a 50 per cent payment by the federal Government of eligible costs of provincial and municipal expenditures for assistance payments, welfare services and health programs. In addition, we cover one-half of the cost of child support services such as foster care, daycare and a broad array of other family and social support services used by Canadians on an ongoing basis.
If Members opposite are still wondering how the money will be spent, I would mention that the Main Estimates also spell out a number of new initiatives undertaken by the Government, including this Small Business Investment Grant Program and the New Employment Expansion Development Plan called the NEED Program, which was touched upon by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) today.
I want to touch upon another criticism that has been raised by Hon. Members in the discussion of this legislation before the House. I am talking about a claim made that the expenditures of the Government, as witnessed by the documents tabled by the President of the Treasury Board, or the funds sought in this legislation, reflect that the Government is not managing or controlling expenditures.
I would remind Hon. Members that the policy and expenditure management system was put in place in 1979 following receipt of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability, the Lambert Commission. That system is in place and is functioning. It was adopted by the Official Opposition when in Government. As Hon. Members are aware, this is a program where spending is
Time Allocation
broken into ten expenditure categories, with Cabinet committees taking responsibility for expenditure management within an envelope system.
Each envelope is provided with a separate policy reserve which functions as a bank account in which unallocated funds are kept. Cabinet committees can add to their policy reserves by cancelling or cutting down on existing programs. Ministers have to vie, argue and debate for the prudent expenditure of funds. Priorities must be struck, and for any expenditure from those funds there is a check and balance.
There are other controls as well. All budgetary appropriations of funds must be approved by Parliament, and the Government supplies very detailed information in the form of Estimates. For example, I have been before the Finance Committee to report on and account for the Department of Insurance which falls under my responsibility, as every other Minister does for the expenditures of his Department.
Parliament must authorize all taxation and borrowing activity by the Government. Within the Government, the Treasury Board rigorously examines all requests for spending authority by Government Departments and agencies. It is constantly on the lookout for inefficiency or impropriety and screens the submission it receives very carefully. I do not think I have to remind Hon. Members of the office of Comptroller-General and the role that he plays in the scheme of things in terms of official management of expenditures of Government.
The Auditor General examines the Government's financial statements very carefully and reports to Parliament on his findings. We were saddened this week with the sudden and unexpected demise of Mr. Macdonnell who took such leadership in this area. He performs a watch-dog function which helps provide further assurance that Government will function according to Parliament's dictates and as efficiently as possible.
Finally, the Government announced in 1975 that henceforth it would endeavour to hold the trend growth in its expenditures to no more than the trend growth in the economy. Over the period from 1975 to 1980, the Government was successful in meeting this objective. In 1981 expenditures rose more rapidly, no doubt a reflection of high interest rates and the consequent effects on public debt charges.
In conclusion, I urge Hon. Members to give speedy disposition to Bill C-143 to permit the Government to meet the real needs of Canadians which I have expressed. We hope this will be done in a most expeditious manner reflecting the efficiency which I detailed in my comments.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-143
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate, I do so with real sorrow. I feel that while the Government has the right to use closure which it is now proposing that the House accept, this is not the time to be using closure on such an important matter as the borrowing requirements of the Government.
I say I rise somewhat in sorrow because, having listened to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove), it is abundantly clear to me that he, and presumably his Cabinet colleagues, have just lost control of the situation. He attempted

March 24, 1983
Time Allocation
to justify the use of closure today on the basis that it is inevitable spending, that somehow they have done their best. To be specific, he said that we put a spending policy in place in 1979 and he feels that things have not been too bad since that scheme was put in place.
Let us not forget the facts. Since this Government took office in February, 1980, just after the 1979 approach that he referred to, Government spending has increased by 68 per cent compared to an increase in the Consumer Price Index of 37 per cent and nominal Gross National Product growth of only 33 per cent.
There can be absolutely no doubt that the public of Canada want and are entitled to a fair debate concerning the Government's borrowing needs, yet we are being denied that. The Minister of State made the comment that after all, Parliament has had 24 hours to debate this matter. I am not too sure whether his arithmetic is correct, but if we divide 24 into $19 billion, we find that he is talking about $800 million per unit. The inference seems to be that after having talked that length of time, let us get on with it.
The Minister is totally ignoring that while there may have been a debate for several hours or days, and I doubt whether it was that long a debate, the fact is that in committee we were denied answers to question after question concerning why the Government needed not only these new funds, but what it had done with some of the funds it has already borrowed. The whole purpose of this forum, this talking House, if you like, this House of Parliament, is that we can debate and hopefully arrive at some consensus as to where suitable changes can be made.
We felt that if the Government needed the $5 billion it was asking for in the current fiscal year, perhaps it should have that authorization. However, we felt there was no need, without understanding more fully what it was going to use the $14 billion for next year, to give it that authority carte blanche. That is our position. To simply say that we have made our point, that somehow or other we have had enough days of debate and the Government is going to bring in closure to get on with it, takes away from Parliament one of its most sacred rights, control, not only of spending, but of borrowing that the Government proposes to do in the name of the people.
The only thing of real substance to which we are entitled in the House is to control Government spending and borrowing. Day in and day out we do not see true democracy in the sense of representative Government but, rather, an elected dictatorship, a dictatorship that goes to the country when they think they can get re-elected on trumped-up issues, so-called charisma. It is an attempt to hoodwink the Canadian public so that they can get back in control and run the country down further and further.
That is why I hope that for once Members will vote the way their conscience tells them to vote on this issue. I hope they will say on this particular point to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of State for Finance that Parliament should be allowed more time, and that, hopefully, some amendments can
be agreed to. I say that because it is most dreadful to look at this Government's handling of our economy.
Let me put this on the record: Looking at the public accounts data for the fiscal year ending 1982-83, we find in the November, 1981 budget the budgetary deficit as a percent of the Gross National Product would be minus 2.8 per cent. That is partly what we are talking of today, Mr. Speaker, this borrowing need, the Government's financial requirement for budgetary deficit. They told us at that time it would be minus 2.8 per cent. In the budget of June, 1982, it was up to minus 5.4 per cent of our GNP. In the financial statement of October, 1982, it was at minus 6.7 per cent of our GNP. And in the update of February, 1983, it had arrived at minus 7.8 per cent of our GNP. Yet we are told that, regardless of how it has misled this House and the public with respect to the current Fiscal year, the Government would like us to sign a blank cheque for another $14 billion to get it through, we are told, until about the summer. The Government is not sure how far this money will take it into next year, but it would like to have it in hand.
The Minister of State for Finance asks how we dare delay passage of this Bill because it may impede the Government's borrowing, taking it for granted that the Government has some right to go out and borrow, and taking it for granted that there should be no questioning of the expenditures which have led us into the malaise which I partly indicated from reading the Government's own figures. But we are now at the point, Mr. Speaker, where one tax dollar in four is used to pay interest on this Government's debt alone. It is phenomenal. If you would like to look at it another way, we are at the point where for every dollar of revenue which the Government now has, it is spending $1.50. One-third, roughly, of the total expenditures at the federal Government level today is being borrowed to pay for it. That is totally wrong.
I have certainly heard Government Members say, "Well, this is what Keynesianism is all about". They believe that somehow if you are in a wrong economic time or in a slump, you should be willing to go into a comparatively larger deficit in order to bring yourself out. But let us look at the facts, Mr. Speaker. If a bigger deficit was going to help, you would think we would have one of the most booming economies in the world. The fact is that in the November, 1981 forecast, the 1982-83 deficit was said to be $10 billion. In June they said it would be $19 billion. In October they said it would be $23 billion, and then finally it was $27 billion. In short, this Government has allowed, in one fiscal year alone, its spending to go from an estimated $10 billion in the red to $27 billion, and what is now touted possibly a $30 billion shortfall.
I mention these things, Mr. Speaker, because I believe when Hon. Members are asked to muzzle Parliament concerning the Bill which is before us, they really must ask themselves why. Why has the Government led us into such a high deficit position? Certainly, our socialists to the left like to talk about these short-term deficits. They, of course, have been one of the
March 24, 1983

supporters of these big deficits which we are now living with. But the fact is that if it is looked upon by the Government, or the socialists, as short-term, we must bear in mind that this federal Government has not balanced its books since 1970, and as the projections indicate, they will be adding another $140 billion in deficits over the next five years.
Since the Liberals have been in power since 1970, the deficit is certainly not a short-term problem. To have a deficit which has added to our net debt in this country some $120 billion in 18 years is a disgrace, and it is certainly the best evidence which we could offer to the Canadian public of the total incompetence and mismanagement of this Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I found the comments of the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) interesting, but passing strange. I found it strange that he should rise and claim that the opportunity for debate was about to be muzzled, when not half an hour ago, when we suggested that on a day next week we would like to have a particular matter debated rather than another, it was he, the Hon. Member for York-Peel, who said, "Absolutely not. You will have no unanimous consent from me to allow that debate to take place". If an Hon. Member had not been thrown out of the House today for saying someone was a hypocrite, there is no telling what words I might have uttered.
In any event, I would like to deal with the problem before us today, that the Government has mismanaged the finances of Canada. The Government has failed to provide the kind of direction in terms of the investment of the finances of Canadians, whether it be finances currently available through taxation and other means, or whether it be finances resulting from borrowing. The Government has failed to establish the proper priorities. Unlike the Hon. Member for York-Peel, who is somewhat myopic about these things and seems to have a serious case of tunnel vision, I do not believe that borrowing in itself is necessarily a bad thing. I am sure that every single Hon. Member of the House of Commons probably has at some time in his life gone to a financial institution and borrowed money. The majority will likely have taken on a mortgage at some point in order to purchase a home, and they have probably been in the process of paying it off over many years. The interesting thing about that is that that kind of borrowing, I would suggest, is appropriate. However, that is not the purpose for which this Government borrows. The Government does not borrow for those kinds of reasons. It has borrowed because its income has fallen off dramatically and, among the many reasons, there is substantial unemployment in the land, which has reduced the tax paid into the coffers of the Government of Canada. Unemployment has reduced the purchasing power of a significantly large number of consumers, and the reduction of that purchasing power has resulted in a decrease in the manufacturing of consumer products in this country. That decrease has resulted in a decrease of the profitability of a large number of small, medium and large companies, and that has resulted again in a reduction in the taxes payable to the Government of Canada. The end result of that has been that
Time Allocation
while the Government's commitments remain not only substantial but grow daily as a result of the high unemployment in the land, its revenues have dropped off dramatically.
If the Government were to come to us and say, "We have in mind a large number of investments which would be undertaken on behalf of the taxpayers of this country." For example, "We intend to rebuild the port facilities, both inland and on the coast. We intend to take a hand building homes at a price that people can afford. We intend to embark upon a program to ensure that the farming community will replace obsolete farm implements and equipment." If the Government would come forward with programs to join with the automobile industry and the Provinces in order to stimulate the capacity of that industry to meet competition and provide a better standard of vehicle at a competitive price for the Canadian public, and that for this purpose, among others, it was going to have to borrow money; if it said it was going to have a complete East-West pipeline built more rapidly than was anticipated so that we could be absolutely self-sufficient in energy in the not too distant future; if it were to say it was going to embark upon a railway redevelopment program for the movement of freight and passengers and to meet the requirements of the next generation; if it came to this House of Commons and said it needed to borrow against future earnings in order to undertake all these things, I think it would find sympathy and support for its request.
I know that, having studied these matters Mr. Speaker, you would undoubtedly agree that a major housing program would put two or three hundred thousand people, now unemployed, back to work during this calendar year. The cost of such a program would be recovered because of the taxes paid by workers and unemployment insurance not paid. The benefits would flow to the community through additional purchasing. The money invested in those homes would be recoverable through mortgage-term payments and rents.
If you were to look beyond that, as I know you have, Mr. Speaker, you would appreciate that if we were to put money in place to encourage the farming community to replace obsolete and inadequate equipment, not only would we be in a better position in the years ahead to meet our commitment to this country's need for food, but to meet our export commitment as well. In addition, people would be put to work at Massey-Ferguson, International Harvester and all the other plants. They would be taken off the unemployment rolls and put on the taxpayer rolls, and would be made a vibrant part of the community. This would instill confidence in the nation.
If we were to engage in the development of the East-West pipeline we could put hundreds if not thousands of steel workers, who are currently unemployed in Saskatchewan and eastern Canada, back to work.
If we were to look at those kinds of programs, if we had a Bill before us to facilitate the borrowing necessary to undertake them, and if we were to measure those undertakings against what it costs now to keep people unemployed, it would be worth what it would cost to have those projects under way

March 24, 1983
Time Allocation
now so that when the recession ends we could get back to building Canada. If we could see that prospect, then the Government would have no trouble; it would not need to move time allocation. We would agree to pass the legislation because the benefits would be both long and short-term. The reason we are so reluctant to hand over the money that the Government is seeking is that it has not provided the justification that we are asking for. We know that its commitment is of little substance. We know that it does not intend to go ahead with projects that will make Canada a better place in the future and make it easier for people to earn a living here.
This not a blind opposition because Hon. Members opposite happen to form the Government and are a bunch of useless Liberals. The Hon. Member for York-Peel's view is so narrow that he cannot see that in any normal business practice, which he constantly refers to, it is quite common to borrow against future needs.
Last night I noticed an announcement that the Steel Company of Canada is issuing new stock options in order to raise working capital, and that other companies are doing likewise.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be taking part in today's debate on the Borrowing Authority Bill and I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to address a matter that has my special interest, namely, the situation of young people in Canada. Ever since I became a Member of this House, Mr. Speaker, I have felt that because of my age, I had a duty to tell our elected representatives, to tell all our colleagues in the House what Canada's young people think and what their concerns are, and to try to be a catalyst, as it were, that would have some effect on the decision-making process.
Mr. Speaker, during these few years, I have had an opportunity, within our existing structures, to propose a series of projects that would to some extent meet the needs of Canada's young people, and the first one on my list is of course the creation of a youth bureau. I am a little disappointed, because we have been discussing the matter for months, for several years even, while our colleagues in the National Assembly have already taken action in this respect, perhaps because they had heard about our ideas or perhaps because their system works faster than ours.
Mr. Speaker, I think that as a Government, we shall very soon have to take a comprehensive view of the problems of young people. Band-aid programs are not going to help. How are we going to respond to the expectations of 600,000 young Canadians who will be looking for jobs this year in June, who will lose any illusions they had about society and the opportunities it was expected to offer, who will realize that their guidance counsellors have misled them and that in the final instance, society is telling them: Listen, you don't have any experience, so why not wait for a while. Wait until the labour market can provide alternatives. Wait until the economy gets back on steam. Meanwhile, however, these young men and women are more or less trapped. They are not entitled to unemployment insurance because as students, they cannot earn unemployment insurance stamps, and so the only alternative they have, unless their families can support them, is to go on welfare.
Or become a Member of Parliament, as my friend Mr. Maltais would say. In Quebec today, there are 75,000 young people who have to live on $140 per month. You know, Mr. Speaker, on $140 per month, you would be a lot thinner, and I think all Hon. Members would be hard-pressed to make ends meet.
Mr. Speaker, with a youth bureau, we would be able to develop a youth policy, once and for all. In 1970, the then Secretary of State, Gerard Pelletier, ordered a committee to prepare a study which was called "It's your turn", and that study has been shelved by the Department of the Secretary of State since 1970. Although I hope it will not take until 1985 before we start looking at the problems of young people, I do hope that 1985 will mark the culmination of a series of successful activities. I am counting on the support of my colleagues on this side of the House, youth being a subject that is very rarely discussed in the House, except by the Liberal caucus.
Our colleagues opposite talk about young people only when their Young Progressive Conservative delegates are in the gallery. Our friends opposite are only concerned about youth when they can make electoral gains, because they know it is not their traditional constituency.
Mr. Speaker, I urgently ask the House to reflect on this subject and to take action. In the weeks to come, we shall have the Speech from the Throne. We shall also have, at least I hope so, the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has promised us. I am convinced it will be possible to instil some innovative thinking in the Throne Speech, and I know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) and many others have submitted a series of proposals to the Minister of Finance that are aimed at easing the strain for these young Canadians who have been disappointed by economic realities.
March 24, 1983

Mr. Speaker, I know this is not a time for extraordinary expenditures, but I am sure that within the Government . .. More than a year ago, an inventory was made of Federal youth programs. I am sure very few young Canadians are aware that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Canadian International Development Agency, the Department of Agriculture, and so forth, have programs that are aimed specifically at young people. The intentory lists eighty-seven programs. Just imagine all the funds earmarked for those programs which could easily be redirected to meet the priorities of the Government and young Canadians.
I would not, however, want to make the same mistake as our provincial friends did, which is to impose programs from the top. I believe that before defining new programs, we should benefit from the experience of those people who would be prepared to work with us and advise us, and this would include groups of young people and others with a lively interest in the problems of young people, who could give us their advice. I am convinced that if the Government and all Hon. Members were to designate a committee of the House that would address itself specifically to the problems of young people and invite them to appear before the committee across Canada, we could certainly redistribute funds to a series of programs that would respond to their priorities.
Mr. Speaker, our education system is experiencing very serious problems, because the dreams of tomorrow have become a nightmare and because after 18, 19, 20 or 21 years of formal schooling, people are unable to obtain jobs. Last week, I was told that 67 per cent of the students who passed their bar examinations were unemployed this year.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Manicouagan has a great sense of humour. I am told that thousands of university graduates who thought they would be able to repay their loans and bursaries, make a career and perhaps get married and have a normal family life, are unemployed and living in poverty.
Mr. Speaker, there is another set of programs relating to physical fitness and amateur sport, and 1 had the privilege of serving as Parliamentary Secretary in that field. 1 finally realized that those programs are only helping the sports elite and that a guy from St-Joachim who wants to learn to play soccer or has a local team cannot apply to the Canadian Government for assistance unless he is outstanding. People talk about the search for excellence, and that bothers me. Today, hundreds of thousands of Canadians need help and they have to get it from their Government, whether it is for recreation, employment or education, and you would think there was no open door policy and no central office for receiving the requests of these young Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I hope we shall very soon be addressing the youth problem in a comprehensive way and that we will avoid taking hasty measures to resolve temporary problems in band-
Time Allocation
aid fashion. I am sure that if all the Members of this House used their imagination, we would be able to find solutions without having to ask taxpayers for more money. Many programs are not sufficiently known, and that is unfortunate. There is tremendous potential within the Federal Government itself. I hope that there will be some restructuring so that young Canadians who had confidence in their Government and still do will not be disappointed.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that our young people will be heard as well. If they are not, our programs will smack of authoritarianism. I think we should avoid the paternalistic or "maternalis-tic" approach that others have taken. From what young people have been saying across the country recently, it is clear they want to be consulted and to be part of the new economic order. I believe this is a challenge that all of us have a duty to meet, and I urgently ask the House to accept some of our suggestions and to address itself to the problems at the top of our priority list.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) who went on in his usual way and said, "It is all right to borrow; after all, everybody else does". I could not help but think of the man who was falling out of the airplane and said, "It's all right, it is not the fall that hurts, it is the impact with the earth; that is the part that hurts". We are at the moment of impact and we are hurting. We are hurting because of the direction in which this Liberal Government and previous Liberal Governments have taken us.
Also I listened with some interest to the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) who said that great things would happen for the young of the country. I too entered the House at what I consider to be a relatively young age; I was in my twenties. I remember fighting the campaign of 1957 and I remember a comment C. D. Howe used. After all, I used it in the 1957 campaign. He said, "What's a million?"

In order to count to $90 billion, which this Government is going to spend, would require 2,853 years. Methuselah, it was said, lived for 965 years. It would take three of his lifetime to count out the $90 billion which this Government is going to spend this year.
Let us look at it another way. Assuming every one of these pieces of paper was $10 billion-and remember that the Government has committed us to $90 billion in expenditures this year-out of that $90 billion we have to set aside two notes, worth $10 billion each, just to service the debt, which is interest on money borrowed.
We are borrowing the equivalent of $30 billion, so we set aside another three of these pieces of paper, and what do we have left? We have $40 billion. That is all we can afford to spend on ourselves today.
What brought us to this situation? I was interested in the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Shefford. He commented on the youth and how he was concerned about them. Let me tell you about my concerns, and let me tell you about my grandparents. When my grandparents came to this country they did not ask the Government for anything except for a chance to work. They did not ask another taxpayer to help them. They tried to stay off the welfare rolls. They were quite prepared to pay their way.
But what has happened in the intervening years with a Liberal Government in power? No matter what we have heard, the Liberal Government has taken us down the road that has led us to where we are today.

I will tell you about John Diefenbaker. I have a few things that I can tell you about John Diefenbaker. In John Diefenbaker's time inflation was under 2 per cent. What do we have now? I can tell you a few more things about John Diefenbaker. I have all the facts here if you give me enough time.
My grandparents came to this country. They were quite prepared to pay their way. But what is happening here today? The Hon. Member says he is concerned about the youth. But who will pay for this borrowing? The youth who are coming onstream are going to be paying. The Hon. Member points to himself. But you are also going to have to point to every young boy or girl in diapers today. They are the ones who are going to have to pay for this. It was all right for any grandparents to pay their way. It is all right for any grandchildren to pay their way, but heaven forbid that the present generation should pay its way.
What is wrong with this society? I have watched what has happened. The last year we had a surplus was in 1969-1970. What happened after that? We have been in a steady decline with deficit after deficit after deficit. From 1958 to 1964 inflation was below 2 per cent. What happened in the 1970s? Hon. Members will remember that Mr. Turner was the Minister of Finance in 1972. Do you remember what happened, Mr. Speaker? He got into an argument with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) because the country was going downhill. Perhaps Mr. Turner knew about it, but he did not stay to fight. He took off into the wild yonder. He left the country to the mercy of the Prime Minister whose only objective was to get elected and throw money at the people telling them that deficits are no problem.
Are deficits no problem? I have already told Hon. Members that in 1969-1970 we had a surplus of $493 million. But in 1970 to 1971 there was a deficit of $372 million. But 1972 the deficit had risen to $702 million. By 1975 John Turner realized the deficit would reach $1.7 billion and he said, "This is enough. I am getting out. I cannot take the responsibility."
Then along came Macdonald, and he said "I will fix it. I will take over." He was given a lot of credit for a lot of intelligence. And so now he has been appointed to solve all our problems. Mr. Macdonald took over as minister of Finance in 1975 and left office in 1977. In two years the deficit jumped from $1.7 billion to $6.2 billion. Now he is going to take three years to tell us what is wrong. I can tell you in two minutes what is wrong. All you have to do is to look at where we are going and where we have been. The only thing the Government has said all along is, "We have to get elected." In 1972 the Liberals ran around the country and said the Conservatives did not have anybody to lead the country. They said to compare Minister for Minister, the Liberals ridiculed the Conservatives. Yes, they ridiculed us.

Yes. We had just a few months. But our projections were that the deficit would go down.
If you look at the graph you will see that as the projections for the deficit go up, so do interest rates. Compare the deficit of $700 million in Mr. Turner's day, which kept on rising, and the interest rates that went all the way up to 21 per cent. When Mr. Turner was here the deficit was $700 million and the interest rate was 6 per cent.
Now let us look at bankruptcies. We have seen 30,000 bankruptcies listed. That situation corresponds and relates to the amount of money the Government spends. Let me remind Hon. Members that the Auditor General told us the Government had lost control of spending.
The cause of the problems that we have today is not the fault of just one Minister; it is the Liberal attitude over the years that has brought this country to its knees. Canada is listed as twenty-fourth of the 24 industrialized countries. How can the Government tell us today that the depression we are in is the fault of the rest of the world? We have heard that statement day in and day out from the Liberals. Successive Liberal Governments, no matter which one is thrown out of office, will continue in the same way. We need a change of Government, a change in attitude, and to make a new start for the sake not only of young Canadians but of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that my remarks in this debate will be of a more positive nature. Of course I respect the right of the Hon. Member who just spoke to dissent in any way he wishes. I believe, however, that in times of difficulty we must not turn our backs on those who are in need. If I understand the Hon. Member's suggestion to be that we should not have that amount of money invested in Unemployment Insurance, I must disagree. If he is suggesting that we should not be using medicare to take care of the people in Canada who are ill, then I must disagree. If we are not going to live up to our commitments to see that our elderly in Canada are taken care of during hard times, then I cannot agree with the Hon. Member's views as he stated them.
This afternoon I would like to address myself, in the short time that I have, to some of the more positive steps that are being taken with the money that the Government is borrowing. I refer generally to the NEED Program and more specifically, to my riding of Welland which is in the Niagara Peninsula.
My riding is basically made up of heavy industry where there is the steel industry and a great number of people who work in the automobile industry. As a result of the decrease in the purchase of cars, the steel industry, automobile industry and other suppliers in the area have slowed down. For that reason there was very high unemployment in the Niagara Peninsula, the St. Catharines region and specifically my Welland riding.
The Government has addressed itself to this problem in two ways. The first way is through the NEED Program. I would point out to Hon. Members that since the NEED Program went into effect, and indeed since December 21, 1983, we in Welland have been the fortunate recipients of moneys to put
March 24, 1983

our people who are exhaustees-those who have run out of Unemployment Insurance benefits-back to work so that they and their families could live normal lives.
Let me refer to the time between December 21 and March 4 when there were 1,785 work weeks created for the people in my riding. In real dollars, this amounted to some $754 thousand without which many families would have gone on welfare. Without this assistance, the savings of many would have been eaten up before they even went on to welfare. These are proud people. If what is being suggested is that the people of Canada do not want to work, then I surely disagree. I do not accept that as a premise. I do not agree that the Government is totally at fault. It goes without saying that we must accept our responsibilities. However, I believe that other segments of our society must also accept their responsibilities.
Rather than shouting at one another back and forth across the floor, there should surely be some constructive proposals. I compliment the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) who suggested that we do need moneys to stimulate the economy moderately. I do not think that the Government has all the solutions and I do not think that unions are all to blame, nor are businessmen. I think that if we put our heads together, we should be able to come up with some solutions.
In the NEED Program, of the $754,000, some $278,000 was for municipal works. Since March 4, another $226,000 has been allocated for municipal works and the non-profit sector, which was at $393,000 on March 4, has also been increased.
I would like to direct the attention of the House to a very exciting project which has been going on in the Welland riding for a year and a half. I hope that some of the moneys being borrowed will be used to further this particular project. I refer, of course, to the Welland Canal Parkway, which is a development project for the city. About a year and a half ago, the Welland Canal Advisory Group was formed to advise City Council and the federal Government, after having held extensive public hearings to determine exactly how these Canal lands should be developed. The Canal was rerouted some 20 years ago, I believe. One part which we now call the old Welland Canal, is approximately eight and a half miles long.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today because we have before us a closure motion involving the borrowing of $19 billion. The Government is now borrowing money by closure and spending money by closure. The Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Parent), who spoke just before me, referred to the beautification of cities. He spoke about parkways becoming pretty and about jobs associated with programs such as the summer work program. We must bear in mind that fact that $19 billion, the sum which is being requested in this borrowing authority Bill, is as much as the total budget for the country when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first became Prime Minister. That debt, in one lump sum of borrowing, is an inexcusable expense, not just to us but also to tomorrow's children. Our future, our tomorrow, has become indebted. Children yet unborn will incur a debt of such magnitude that they will hardly be able to escape. They will bear an extraordinary burden.
In effect, the Canada summer works program is one which all Members of Parliament should stand to oppose, irrespective of the good work it may do in their community, such as the moving of grass, the pruning of trees, the fixing of golf courses, the painting of graveyards, the fixing up of the halls. That is an absolute waste of money. This country needs an engine, and the Government has killed the main engine of this country's economy. It has killed the oil industry.
The Government, with its former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his new National Energy Program, drove rig after rig out of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I believe that many persons did not even know what we were talking about when we spoke of moving an oil rig out. They thought that maybe a truck left with a derrick on it. Consider some 16 to 20 big, long liner trucks, with compressors, costing $500,000 a move to go from Alberta into the United States. We lost half of our drilling capacity within just a short period after that
program was announced. Government killed the engine of society.
It has been said, "Well, that is Alberta. Who cares? What does it matter if Alberta is killed?" I bring to Your Honour's attention the fact that one tar sands plant, in 25 years of production, promotes $108 billion in direct spending in the Province of Ontario. It does that in steel; it does that in transportation equipment; it does that in its spin-off of manufacturing. And the Government killed the engine. What is the Government's response? How do we justify borrowing $19 billion?
The Hon. Member for Welland stands up and says the Welland Canal Parkway might get some more money out of this borrowing. He is hoping that if we borrow more money his community of Welland will look prettier. Who cares if it looks prettier? What this country needs is to get the engine of this country working so that the people in every community will have the capacity to make their communities look prettier and to do that out of their own initiative, not out of borrowed money. We are in the position today in which every time we pay a tax dollar, 25 cents goes to pay the interest on our foreign debt. Out of every four dollars, we have to pay a dollar for nothing, for nothing except to pay for interest, and that, Sir, is not worth making communities pretty. We have to have more capacity than that to develop our country.
We are in a situation today in which the only reason we are surviving is because we are an educated nation that is resource rich. Our per capita debt is seven times greater than that of Latin America. If you look at Mexico, Brazil, Venezuela-any one of those 22 nations in the southern hemisphere or the Latin American block, including Brazil, a Portuguese-speaking country-you will find Sir, that we no longer may use loosely the expression that we are a "banana republic". Our debt is sevent times greater per capita than that of Latin America and, countries such as Mexico, with a population many times larger than that of Canada, which have an accumulated debt of only $80 billion. Here we are with a debt of $140 billion to divide among 24 million people.
We should be ashamed. Debt upon debt upon debt, borrowing upon borrowing; virtually every few months this Government is back asking to borrow more money. Now they are borrowing more money, and $14 billion of the $19 billion that they are borrowing are to be spent at some future time, in a new fiscal year, for which there is not a budget. What is a budget? A budget is a plan for how you are going to spend your money. They are asking us, under the threat of closure, to authorize $14 billion, and they have not even outlined to the people of Canada why they need it or how they are going to spend it. Then they became hostile and upset and they burn with indignation and say that we are holding up the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, why was this House of Commons started in the first place? It started because at the time of the Magna Carta, more than 700 years ago, the subjects of the time, when
March 24, 1983

the king was all-powerful, did not like the fact that he wanted to build a new castle and tax the already over-burdened subjects one more time. They rebelled against him. They gave him a choice, and the choice was that he was to be stripped of power and power was to come to the common people, and if it did not, he would lose his head. Being a wise king, he chose the former. We had common people with power, and that is why we are a House of Commons, because we are a place of common people. This is no longer a House of Commons and it is no longer a Parliament of power because the power is not among its individual Members who represent their constituencies; it is among those 30-some people who sit in the Cabinet. By closure they borrow, and by closure they spend. They do it by closure. They strip from the people of Canada their base of power, and now they want some $19 billion without a budget, without a plan, without a reason or a rationale. They are simply saying to us that they want some more money because the Cabinet believes that they have a way for spending more money. That, Mr. Speaker, takes us from the role of citizen to the role of subject. It is not now what the Parliament and its representatives believe is right, it is what that Cabinet thinks is right; it is the king again. It is back to King Charles I- whatever he wants. This Cabinet believes that they have this almighty power to dream whatever they want to, whether it is fixing up the pretty flowers in Welland or any other community, just to borrow more money, the justification for $19 billion. What a terrible excuse the Hon. Member for Welland has put before us today for the borrowing of some $19 billion!
The Auditor General, just a few years ago, was telling us that this Government had lost control of the public purse and, more recently, the Auditory General is telling us that not only do we need to be concerned about the waste and the overexpenditure of Government, but that there is a whole subGovernment starting, and a sub-Government that is not accountable, he said as he pointed his finger at Crown corporations. There are some 480 Crown corporations wholly or partially owned by the federal Government. There are 274 Crown corporations wholly owned by the federal Government. With a record like that, obviously, with those Crown corporations not accountable to our Public Accounts, not coming before Committee and not standing the test or the scrutiny, naturally this Parliament remember that the reason it was formed was for the control of the purse-has lost that power, and that fact is stripping power from the citizens of this country. That is where power should be, in the House of Commons, for common people. Instead, what we have is a Cabinet that borrows under closure and spends under closure, assuming unto itself all rights and all privileges.
Mr. Speaker, that defies our history; it defies our rationale; it defies the purpose of this place and it defies, most of all, the individual Canadians from coast to coast and their Gob-given right to presume that in democracies they are powerful. In fact what has happened is that that group of some 30 persons on the other side has now made it so that our debt is seven times larger than the per capita debt of Latin America. We are

And so, Mr. Speaker, they sell out tomorrow; they mortgage children yet unborn; they put a debt on them for the purpose of existing to make Welland pretty today.
If we started to build the engines of this economy-

Mr. Speaker, 1 might well start with the beautification of Welland, why we would be concerned with the beautification of Welland, and why this Government should be concerned with summer employment plans that will have young people out cutting grass, painting and fixing things up.
I think that the previous speaker, while he spoke about a Canada from coast to coast, seemed to concentrate on one area of the land, without thinking in the broad perspective of what Canada is all about.
First of all, it is a young country, still growing, and, as a growing country, it has required a lot of extraordinary investments. More important, I believe that we need the money that we are asking for today and we have to put some time allocation on the debate because it is necessary to have that money flowing, for very good reasons, as soon as possible.
I think Canada is what it is today because we have learned, in our peculiarly Canadian way, that somehow we can find ways for each region of the country to help out other regions, recognizing that it is the totality of the land, working together, and the interaction that has come out of necessity between Governments and the private sector, that have brought us to the stage at which we are today. When I look around, I do not think that we have done all that badly by any standard.
To go back to the employment program, which I am anxious to see re-started in northwestern Ontario this summer and in all parts of the land, the previous speaker spoke about the engine that fueled the economy and said that we have killed it. What really fuels a country is people. The Hon. Member made reference to how well educated we are. I cannot find fault with a plan that creates an opportunity to beautify the land, something which has an aesthetic value, a morale-building quality, and a pragmatic value. This is particularly so as one of our prime industries is tourism. In order to have a tourist industry, you must have an attractive package for the tourist to view.
I cannot see anything wrong with a program of giving some kind of assistance to young people who will be returning to their studies in the fall. They will be those well-educated people of whom the Hon. Member spoke. They will in fact give even greater impetus to the future of our country because they are better educated.
I hope that their education will include learning about the area in which they live, whether it be Alberta or southwestern

March 24, 1983
Time Allocation
Ontario. The charge is sometimes made that that education is lacking in this country. I regret to say it is sometimes lacking in this House. I repeat, education must include a recognition of the regions of this country.
Much has been made about the National Energy Program. It has been said that it caused the death of that very important industry and, to quote the previous speaker, the country does not give a damn. We must remember that the oil industry grew up in this country because the people of Canada supported and promoted it. People seem to quickly forget the large tax advantages given to that industry. I do not regret that because this did help to build the industry. We sometimes neglect to see that most of what is going on in that industry, which is depressed world-wide, which includes our friends to the South who are having immense difficulties, is the result of the National Energy Program, because Petro-Canada is taking a lead role in this area.
We are in the position of having to ask to borrow a great deal more money. Along with every other Member in this House, I regret the necessity of a deficit, of not having enough money in the bank to do all the work at this time. I believe that, by and large, the money spent by the Government over the last few years has been done in a reasonable and equitable fashion across this land in order to accomplish a number of things. It has helped those Members of our society who are neglected to enjoy a fair and reasonable share of the wealth of this land. We have tried to help our senior citizens who did not have the opportunity to build a pension plan or the wherewithal to take them through their twilight years. We tried to use some of the resources to help people with medicare and other programs of that nature. It is expensive. Had we not taken those actions, the hardships in this land would be far more severe than they now are. I refer to the Unemployment Insurance plan. The Government and the people of Canada are in the difficult position of having declining revenues at a time when we need to carry on this very necessary service. This necessary growing deficit position has been created for a brief period of time.
I believe that some of the programs for which this money will be used will hasten our extraction from our present difficult position. That money will flow into such programs as the NEED Program which assits those whose benefits have run out, the summer employment program, and other programs of that nature. In addition, it is tremendously important because it will help provide the infractructure to enable us to continue to grow more quickly in the future. The dollars that we provide through such programs as the NEED Program, meagre as they may seem at times, create a spin-off. If a dozen people are employed on a project in downtown Nipigon make purchases to complete their work, it will create a spin-off effect for that business community. The number of dollars may seem small because so often we deal in such large sums of money. However, to a small community, these supposedly small sounding amounts are big dollars. They make the difference between success and failure.
I would love it if we were in a position of not having to borrow more money. However, I support the idea of having these funds on hand to meet current obligations so that we can continue carrying out programs that assist the economy. As the economy grows, we can then concentrate on reducing the deficit.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister responsible for this Bill referred to the great number of Members of Parliament who had spoken on the Bill. I had the privilege of speaking before. I now want to say a few words on closure or time allocation, the more gentlemanly term which means the same thing.
Those of us in Opposition are well aware that this is a bad Bill. If some of those on the other side would think on a purely non-partisan basis, they would raise their eyebrows about a Bill which demands of this House $19 billion. We have demonstrated that a borrowing Bill of this size and nature is clearly unprecedented, either in Canada or elsewhere in the parliamentary world. We have shown time after time that it is a bad Bill, one that promises to mortgage the future of Canadians to a greater extent than either we, or indeed most certainly they, are aware.
The list goes on. These are all bad things. We all realize that, and once again that must include Members of the back benches across the aside. After all, they should think seriously about the matter and consider it objectively.
Being a bad Bill does not make it an anomaly among Bills put forward by this Government. Anything but! Certainly it being a bad Bill is not enough to get me on my feet so often. There is more. This Bill goes right to the heart of what we Members of Parliament are here for. It strikes right at the roots of the parliamentary system and the principles upon which it is based.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) mentioned earlier that in 1649 a king was executed. It was the only time in my memory that such a thing has been done by due process of law in the history of our monarchy. Why was this terrible thing done? It was because the King, Charles I, had been the loser in a struggle over who was to control access to the public purse. It took a civil war to establish that henceforth in the parliamentary system, Parliament, and Parliament alone, would have the authority to allot moneys which came from the pockets, the livelihood, the sweat of the body and the fruit of the brains of the taxpaying public. What is more, this was not to be a token control, to be voted at the whim of the executive, be that executive of Royal or of Cabinet form. Parliaments everywhere, until the introduction of this Bill, have jealously guarded the right to examine the purposes toward which it is being asked to vote public money.
Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that I am not claiming this authority for the Official Opposition, nor for the Opposition as a whole. This is the authority, this is the right, this is the sovereign right of Parliament. And that places a very heavy
March 24, 1983

onus upon us all, but perhaps especially upon those Members of the Government who are not bound by the bonds of a Cabinet oath. I sympathize with those Hon. Members. I sympathize with them very much, because, having sat in this place with them for as long as I have, I know what a strain they must be under, as they ponder the relative weights of their twin responsibilities; to their Party and its long tradition of valuing the exercise of power above all else, and to the parliamentary and democratic system and what their support of this Bill will do to it.
Above all else, Mr. Speaker, we are establishing a parliamentary precedent with this Bill. If we pass it, we are saying that 300 years of parliamentary history-over 100 of them spent right here between these four walls-are for naught! We are saying that no longer does Parliament rule supreme, nor do the people, whose only legitimate representative we collectively are. We are saying that Charles I rides again in the persons of the Liberal Cabinet of the Member for Mount Royal, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). More specifically, we are saying that we shall have to codify exactly the behaviour which we expect from our Governments in the future, because any Government that follows the precedents established by this one, will refuse to be controlled by any traditions, precedents or codes of behaviour which are not written down, preferably on stone. We are gathered here to authorize, or more accurately to rubberstamp, the purloining of more money from the public pocket than was paid for the entire operation of the federal Government, its activities, its programs, all that it did, a scant dozen years ago.
This is in the form, not of a budget but of the authority to borrow on the public markets, with no further questions asked, $19 billion, which will have to be repaid with high interest out of the public pocket, and most critically for the future of the system of Government we profess to espouse, with no indication whatsoever as to what purposes the funds are to be put. Mr. Speaker, I am not a dogmatist, nor am I dyed-in-the-wool reactionary who will fight against change purely for the purpose of maintaining the status quo of the good old days. That type of thinking surely has no place in these times of such fast-paced changes. But the record of this Government, this Cabinet, in matters of constitutional self-discipline is not encouraging.
This is the Government of a Prime Minister who, when asked how far he would go in suppressing human rights in response to a kidnapping in Quebec, replied, "Just watch me". This is the successor Government to one which, having been defeated in the House, decided it was all a joke and rewrote the "gentlemen's agreement" upon which such things had been based until that time. This is the Government for whom, more than any other, time allocation and closure have become a way of life. Seventeen times so far have they been applied during this session alone, and more to come. This is the Government whose Leader described Members of Parliament as "just nobodies when they are 50 yards away from Parliament Hill". Be that as it may, "nobodies" or not, we are the men and women who are charged by our electors with the protection of their purse. No one else has that authority. No one else has that responsibility. Regardless of our Party affiliations, if we
Time Allocation
support this Bill and allow it to pass, we are spitting in the eyes of those who sent us to this place.
Some of you, more particularly those who are trying desperately to ignore the constitutional implications of the Bill, will be trying to pretend that I am making a mountain out of a molehill. You will be trying to tell yourselves that all of this constitutional nonsense is just that, nonsense. Yet, no longer than a few hours ago, the division bells rang loud and long, calling us to vote on the heinous matter of a Member having used "unparliamentary language". That is a parliamentary no-no. Yet we all now what he meant, and his alteration of the words he used to say it really could not have mattered less. But we went through the song and dance of a vote. Is it not of much greater importance to protect the right of the taxpaying public and let them know why their money is being taken from them before the deed is done? I ask you, Parliamentarians on all sides of the House not to let this Bill pass.
There was a very sad announcement in this House that a former Auditor General, J. J. Macdonell, had passed away suddenly. He had been a great servant of the House. I believe it was mentioned earlier this afternoon, that he had pointed out forcefully that Parliament had lost control of the public purse. Whether this can be blamed on Cabinet or whether it can be blamed on the bureaucrats who are the ones bringing forth this legislation, we are still faced with being asked for a blank cheque for $19 billion, and we should say an emphatic no to this.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in this debate on the closure motion with respect to the borrowing authority of $19 billion which the Government has put before us to be approved. The Government is asking for this borrowing authority so that it can borrow money and possibly put us further into debt than we already are. The accumulated national debt by the end of this year will be somewhere in the area of $160 billion. I believe that is a sad state of affairs, and I can honestly say that I do not know that it is a political problem, to a large extent. I believe that could happen today under almost any Government in Canada, as sad as that may be.
It was mentioned in the debate a little earlier, Mr. Speaker, that the people of the country are really the most valuable resource of the country, and I agree with that. The people are the most valuable resource that we have, but it seems to me that they have less and less input into what is happening within this country through their representatives in Parliament. I do not put any blame on the Liberals or the Conservatives, necessarily, but I believe that we are rapidly coming to a point when many Canadians are losing faith in the institution of Parliament, and in having their vote really count for something when they send a Member of Parliament to represent them in the federal House of Commons, to speak on their behalf and to have a hand in dealing with the affairs of the country.
There seems to be a real lack of democracy within this institution when we have a majority Government elected, as we

March 24, 1983
Time Allocation
do now, because a majority Government in Canada can do anything it wants. It can change Saturday to Sunday, if it so wishes. It could call a dollar a metric tool. Anything can happen here because there is no check and balance beyond this House, as there should be, and that would be the upper House or the Senate of Canada. The reason that the Senate is not a check and balance to this Government is that by far the greatest number of Members in the Senate are appointed because of their partisan contributions to a political movement within this country. That is a sad state of affairs, Mr. Speaker. We should have an elected Senate. Perhaps that would ensure more democracy under a majority Government. I will have more to say about an elected Senate later.
First of all, I should like to point out that in this Chamber, Members of Parliament have little, if any, influence. Of course, we work on behalf of our constituents and assist them with pension or immigration problems and all the concerns that they have when dealing with the Government. People often approach their elected representatives for help with those problems and in many cases we are successful in helping them. But we have very little influence in this House, Mr. Speaker. In reality, we can do nothing this afternoon to stop this closure motion from passing, even if that were the will of most Members of Parliament.
The changes that have taken place over the years have a great deal to do with the media, I believe, and with the transportation system that we have built up in the country. For example, I would be surprised if there were more than two or three Members of Parliament in the House at the moment, listening to what I am saying.

In the early days, things were much different. From the time of Confederation until World War II there was not a great media coverage of the country, nor was there rapid transportation such that Members could travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific in one day. Until World War II, if a Member of Parliament made a speech in this House, the other Members took a great deal of interest in it. In that way a Parliamentarian was able to deliver a message to Members from other parts of the country. They listened because they were concerned about the country. Now, with rapid communication and rapid transportation, Members do not have to really listen to each other. They can pick up the morning paper and read the report of a journalist from some other part of the country, or they can hop on an airplane and travel to any part of the country to witness an event at first hand.
That is a sad situation, Mr. Speaker, and it points out that in a way this institution has become archaic and that some of the systems with which we operate should be changed. I do not think it is just a matter of changing Governments-that one Government would be more efficient or administer the country
better than another; it is a matter of changing the systems under which we work.
One thing that would improve our systems and enhance democracy in this country would be an elected Senate. In the House of Commons we have representation through population, and that is fair. But in a country as large as this, it seems to me that there should be some regional representation as well so that areas with the majority of population cannot impose something on outlying parts of the country without some check and balance being in place. One way to achieve that would be to have an elected Senate with equal numbers of Senators from each Province and the Territories elected to serve in the Upper House. When legislation passes this House, particularly when there is a majority Government which may not have listened to opposing views, the Senate could examine it from a regional perspective and make any changes that might be necessary. If that were the case I do not think that today we would be arguing about whether the Government should be able to borrow money when it does not have a plan or does not tell us the plan or because, some would say, it is incompetent-I think if all that were set aside we could get on with running the country in a more democratic way.
Democracy seems to prevail only at election time. Between elections there is very little democracy in the country. That is a sad state of affairs for this institution and for the country. Democracy is a basic right. People must have some say in the systems that run the country, even in cases where they disagree.
Members of the New Democratic Party-and I was one of them-opposed the testing of the Cruise missile. When we spoke about that this afternoon in the House some Hon. Members said that they did not want to debate it in the House. I think that is wrong, Mr. Speaker. In a democracy we listen to everyone. People must have a forum in which to express their concern. As we have seen in other countries, when this is denied them, revolutionary forces spring up. I hope we never see that in Canada.
The ancient philosopher, Voltaire, said something to the effect that, "I may disagree profoundly with what you have to say but 1 will defend to the death your right to say it." We should keep that in mind, Mr. Speaker, and not criticize each other's motives in this House. We should listen to each other and try to make the country a better place to live and prosper. No country in the world has the potential of Canada. As a Member of Parliament, I would not want to be part of anything that would destroy that future for my children or their children.
We should get on with doing the job and look for new systems under which we can operate more effectively rather then apportioning blame. That is not actually the problem.

Mr. Speaker, on March 15 1 addressed a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) in respect to the make work programs which are in place for the various constituencies of Canada. I asked that question in this House because I
had received a letter on February 25 from the Minister advising me that the last date that applications for any of the Summer Works programs should be in was March 4. March 25 happened to be a Friday and the letter arrived in my office after I had left. I therefore did not learn of the closing date until the following Monday.
Mr. Speaker, in a constituency such as yours and mine, a great deal of the information is circulated via the weekly paper. There was no way at the time of that late announcement that 1 could advise the people of Carleton-Charlotte that the closing date for the summer works type of program would be March 4. 1 therefore asked the Minister, inasmuch as it was impossible for the constituents of Carleton-Charlotte to know of the closing date in time to get applications in, would he extend that date by two weeks.
1 then went to the trouble of asking of the weeklies and of organizations if they had had any notice of any kind as to when the closing date was for applications for this program. The answer was no, they had had no notification. I then called the officials of the Department, for my constituency, and was advised that there would be no extension after that date of March 4. This meant that many organizations had no way of knowing that the closing date was in fact March 4.
I repeated my question later in the House and again asked for an explanation. I was again advised that I should be the individual to advise the constituents of Carleton-Charlotte and all its organizations that the closing date was to be March 4. That was impossible. This has rendered a hardship to the constituents who might have applied, as well as to the various organizations that might have applied.
I think Hon. Members know that the various organizations promoting the interests of our native people have pretty good communication with the various Ministers, first through the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), and then through their own information centres, as to when they can apply for the benefits of programs.
Last week an Indian Chief from New Brunswick was in my office. He stated that he had not been notified of the closing date, that he had not made an application and that he was advised by the officials of the Department of Employment and Immigration that there was no way that an application from his Band could be accepted for projects for summer work. In addition to that, and this is a side issue, he was advised that his budget was being sharply reduced by the Department of Indian Affairs. He stated that a combination of the two situations wreaked very serious hardship upon him, his Band and his officials.
I was not the only one who did not know. I took the opportunity on the first Tuesday in March to ask other Members if they knew of the closing date for applications for the summer employment programs. The answer was no in every instance.
I mentioned in my question, and I repeat it again, this Government has budgets known to be in the vicinity of $300

million for advertising. The cost of advertising through the various little pamphlets that come out far exceeds that item. I submit it is incumbent upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration in the future to properly advertise any program and the closing date for applications, giving not less than three weeks public notice of that closing date. This is in the best interest of the people we are trying to serve, particularly the student population of Canada which does not have a hope of getting in those applications to get the work they so badly need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few
minutes at my disposal, I shall try, to the best of my ability, to give some explanations to the Hon. Member in connection with his complaints about the advertising of the Summer Canada program. First of all, perhaps I may say that I too represent a rural constituency, and that the problems encountered by the Hon. Member in his own constituency are perhaps even greater in my own, considering its boundaries which include the Magdalen Islands, where communications are certainly a problem.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister announced the Summer Canada program in December. He made it clear that the program was available to students across Canada, that application forms would be available in all Canada Employment Centres and that starting in the middle of January, all Canada Employment Centres and their officers would be asked to promote the program in their respective areas.
The advertising campaign in our dailies and weeklies throughout the land started on February 14, and 1 think it was clearly indicated that the closing date for applications would be March 4. Following this advertising campaign, our officials visited most ridings to promote this program and show the students how to submit applications. It is true that the Hon. Member asked the Minister in the House for an extension of the application period, which was granted. The Minister later announced that applications would be accepted until March 14 from coast to coast. Moreover, all our officials and Canada Manpower Centers were advised that the closing date had been postponed and that they should make sure that all interested parties were made aware of that extension.
This question was asked in the House, Mr. Speaker, and was answered by the Minister, Mr. Speaker, precisely to make sure that Hon. Members would refer to Hansard and would read the announcement made by the Minister, so that in turn they could advise all those concerned. It was very difficult, in that ten day period, to return to the newspapers, especially the weeklies, and ask them to carry this announcement. That is why the Minister chose the House, a public forum, to inform Canadians that the closing date for submitting application had been postponed.
