NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS-CANADIAN POSITION ON GENEVA ARMS CONTROL TALKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) what proposals Canada would be putting forward when Vice-President Bush came to Ottawa,

March 24, 1983
Adjournment Debate
which he did yesterday, in connection with the Geneva negotiations on intermediate nuclear missiles. The Minister said that Canada would be putting forward some proposals. He was not specific.
When I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today what those principles were he referred me to the speech he gave last night in which there was a suggestion that Canada would support something less than the famous zero option previously proposed by President Reagan. It seems clear that the zero option is not going to be accepted and that something new will come along. What is the change, Mr. Speaker? What would Canada propose to solve the terrible difficulty of avoiding the nuclear precipice that the arms race has hurtled us toward?
In his speech last night the Prime Minister further confused the issue by talking about the Cruise missile, this time suggesting the Government had an obligation to NATO. This is a change from the previous presentation of the issue in which it was presented in bilateral terms as a request from the United States. At one stage we heard that a request was made and, indeed, the former Secretary of State for External Affairs said a commitment had been made in principle. That was later denied by the Prime Minister and the present Secretary of State for External Affairs.
We do not know whether the Canadian Government has given serious consideration to testing the Cruise missile vehicle delivery system because, by the words of the three Ministers I have named, the Government has deliberately obfuscated the issue so that now the Canadian people have no clear idea of where we stand on the nuclear arms question.
There is a tremendous surge of public opinion in the country, of which, undoubtedly, the Government is aware. However, I think the Government is remiss in its duty to give leadership to the Canadian people on this extremely important question. It is also negligent in not taking an initiative as one of a group of nations forming part of NATO that wants to put pressure on the two super powers having 95 per cent of all nuclear technology and armaments between them. The rest of the world is being held hostage today to the never-ending arms race.
Last night the President of the United States gave a new version of Star Wars-that so far has been fiction-but now in the closing years of this century, we are going to be hurled into a form of outer space use of laser beams in a defensive capacity. That would only lead to an increase in armaments, when the central point of all of this is the negotiations now going on in Geneva, and what is being done to put pressure on both parties on behalf of humanity. That is the question I put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to the Prime Minister. But we do not get any answers.
There is total confusion on the issue of the Cruise. On the essential issue, I believe Canada should put forward initiatives that would be realistic, given the over-all premise that existing nuclear capabilities in the world are sufficient to ensure the
credibility of nuclear deterrents, and that nuclear modernization, beyond where we are now, could lead us to a new round in the strategic and nuclear arms race. In other words, if we are going to support a strategy of suffocation, then I believe we must be true to that.
If Canada wants to put forward some proposals, we should propose that the United States and the Soviet Union jointly announce a bilateral moratorium on the flight testing of all nuclear weapons' systems. Such a moratorium would remain in effect during the Geneva negotiations on nuclear arms reductions between the United States and the Soviet Union. That is an essential policy that would drive straight to the heart of the matter and stop all this fooling around about whether to test Cruise missiles and what our obligations are.
Our obligations are clear, Mr. Speaker. We have an obligation to participate in NATO but we also have an obligation to mankind and to the human condition. Today, as an important leading nation in the world we must make realistic proposals. I believe that at the United Nations Canada should support the proposals that have already been made.
The first proposal is an immediate halt by all nations to the testing, deployment and production of all nuclear weapons and delivery systems, pending major reductions in nuclear arsenals. The second is that there be negotiations aimed at achieving a world treaty for simultaneous, balanced, verifiable and enforceable arms reductions, eventually to the minimum level of police forces required for internal security. That was at the heart of the document produced by the First Special Session on Disarmament of the United Nations in 1978. That document contains a comprehensive program for disarmament in the world. Sadly, it has not been implemented because of a continued escalation of the arms race, rather than the nations of the world, Canada chief among them, banding together to force progress in negotiations in Geneva and, indeed, in all five sets of these ongoing complicated negotiations.
In his first report, the Secretary General of the United Nations, Mr. Perez de Cuellar, said, "We are perilously near to a new international anarchy". I believe the Canadian Government ought to be listening to that man and acting accordingly.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS-CANADIAN POSITION ON GENEVA ARMS CONTROL TALKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always very interested in the comments of the Hon. Member for Edmonton South, but I would like to put this discussion in the proper context.
In 1977, the Soviet Union deployed its first intermediate-range nuclear missiles, the SS-20s, which were equipped with three nuclear warheads and had a range of 5,000 kilometers, and by so doing threatened all Western European cities. At the request of the European Allies and my Hon. colleague mentioned earlier that this was a bilateral agreement but it was certainly at the request of our Western European Allies,
March 24, 1983

NATO decided in 1979, under the Government of my Hon. colleague, who is now trying to take the side of virtue and motherhood, to deploy new intermediate-range missiles to replace shorter-range missiles because of the threat posed by the SS-20s. At the same time, NATO suggested to the Soviet Union that mutual restrictions be negotiated on these missiles.
There is therefore nothing new about the theories of my hon. colleague. The visit of Vice-President Bush gave us an opportunity to discuss the progress which was accomplished in the negotiations now under way in Geneva. In 1979, the members of NATO had suggested the zero-zero option, which would consist in eliminating completely the entire class of intermediate-range missiles, both on the side of the Soviet Union and the United States. We are still convinced that this would be ideal since this type of missile would be completely eliminated. NATO never considered this solution impossible or inflexible. In consultation with the other members of NATO, we are now examining the feasibility of proposing a new approach to bring about a compromise agreement which would not be all virtue
Adjournment Debate
and motherhood, but which would at least allow the negotiations to proceed so that balance in this type of arms can be achieved at the lowest possible level. If NATO decides to take this new approach, we plan to keep in mind the ultimate objective of wiping out these missiles completely. We hope that there will eventually be a second agreement to this end. At the meeting between Mr. Bush and the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), we expressed the concerns of this Government and the people of Canada and the wish that the negotiations will now proceed more quickly. As this might involve greater flexibility, we are now consulting our allies in this regard and we hope that such flexibility can lead to profitable negotiations and the maintenance of world peace if possible so that we may never face a nuclear war.
